newsitem.title: ITALY: Dini says Italy won't accept half-baked EU reform.
newsitem.headline: Dini says Italy won't accept half-baked EU reform.

text.p: Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini signalled on Tuesday that Italy would not accept a rushed reform of the European Union's workings and institutions based on what he called "minimalist solutions".

In an article for Corriere della Sera newspaper, he said negotiations under way ahead of a crucial EU summit in June that is scheduled to agree a new treaty could be the bloc's last chance for real reform before its planned eastward expansion.
Failure to agree proper reform could jeopardise the enlargement process itself, Dini wrote.

"The time has therefore come to caution that there are objectives which cannot be renounced, aims which Italy has not been the only country to raise, even if at times it has done so more loudly than the others."

He cited the need for a common foreign and security policy, efficient decision-making by the EU's executive Commission, more majority voting and more opportunity for some member states to move faster towards integration than others.

"European governments...could be tempted to close the chapter of institutional reform in a hurry, to accept minimalist solutions. That would be a very dangerous temptation and one that would make the very enlargement of the Union fraught with risks and difficult to achieve."
Dini wrote that the drive towards a single European currency, which the EU says will go ahead in January 1999, was not the only ambition Europe should consider.
"The moment has come to remember that we face tests which do not just concern the currency," he said.
"We must all respect the rules of virtuous finances but they are not the only ones that exist...there are also other parameters (that) Italy will watch just as closely.

"We therefore want to signal them, with great frankness, to our partners and underline that there cannot be any softening or delay on them either. It's worth saying that now so that there aren't any surprises," Dini wrote.

The article was timed to coincide with the start of a two-day meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg at which Dini and his colleagues will discuss progress in the inter-governmental conference (IGC) on the EU's workings.

The IGC review, launched at a special summit in Turin, northern Italy, in March last year, is aimed at wide-ranging treaty reforms to prepare the 15-member bloc for an ambitious expansion into former communist eastern Europe.
It has become bogged down over how to re-shape the executive Commission and ensure a fair weighting of member states' votes in the decision-making process.
EU heads of government are due to meet in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 to agree a new treaty, paving the way for accession talks with a number of ex-communist states.

Italian diplomatic sources said Dini's article was intended to sound the alarm amid concerns in Rome that some countries were being tempted to rush reforms so as not to delay expansion plans and reopen the negotiations in a few years' time.

The sources said the article should not be seen as a threat to use an Italian veto in Amsterdam nor as establishing a link between reform and Italy's hopes of joining a single currency. "There is no trade-off," one source said.
